The Bacchae. Euripides' final masterpiece, a tragedy of religious ecstasy, divine vengeance, and the dangerous boundaries between civilization and nature. It's a play about what happens when you deny a god, and that god decides to punish you.

Pentheus is the king of Thebes, a man of reason and order. Dionysus, the god of wine, ecstasy, and theatre, has arrived in the city, but Pentheus refuses to acknowledge him as divine. He denies the cult. He forbids the worship. This refusal is Pentheus's fatal mistake.

Dionysus, in disguise as a young priest, sets his revenge in motion. He drives the women of Thebes—including Pentheus's own mother, Agave—into bacchic frenzy. They abandon the city and gather on Mount Cithaeron, wild and ecstatic, dancing themselves into a state beyond reason or restraint.

Pentheus is curious. He wants to spy on the rites. Dionysus, still disguised, seduces him into going, dressed in woman's clothing, to observe the sacred mysteries. It's a trap. When the bacchantes see him, they don't recognize him as their king. In their ecstatic frenzy, they believe he's a wild animal—a lion or some creature threatening their god. They tear him limb from limb.

Agave, Pentheus's mother, leads the attack. In her ecstatic state, she carries her son's head aloft as a trophy, believing she has captured the head of a lion. When she comes back to herself—when the ecstasy fades and she recognizes what she holds—her devastation is complete. She realizes she has murdered her own child.

The play presents Dionysian worship as both ecstatic liberation and violent transgression. Euripides blurs all boundaries—male and female, civilization and wilderness, reason and ecstasy. Pentheus tries to control reality through logic and law, but Dionysus proves that the world cannot be controlled, that human nature contains forces far more primal than reason can contain. Whether Dionysus is righteous or monstrous remains ambiguous. The play simply shows what happens when divinity is denied, and what the cost of that denial can be.
